subject: environmental-science
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which process returns carbon to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide?
questions.explain: Combustion of fossil fuels, like respiration and decomposition, releases stored carbon back to the atmosphere as CO2.

questions.q: r-strategist species are typically characterised by:
options: Stable populations close to carrying capacity
Few offspring with high parental care and long lifespans
Many offspring, rapid reproduction, small body size and little parental care
questions.explain: r-strategists produce many small offspring quickly with little parental care, enabling rapid colonisation of unstable environments.

questions.q: Ecological efficiency between two trophic levels is best defined as the:
options: Number of species at a trophic level
Ratio of energy passed on to a level to the energy received by the level below it
questions.explain: Ecological efficiency is the proportion of energy received at one trophic level that is passed on to the next, typically around 10%.

questions.q: Denitrifying bacteria in the nitrogen cycle are responsible for:
options: Converting nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen gas
questions.explain: Denitrification by denitrifying bacteria converts soil nitrates into nitrogen gas, returning nitrogen to the atmosphere.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen fixation is the conversion of:
options: Atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia or ammonium
questions.explain: Nitrogen fixation converts inert atmospheric N2 into ammonia or ammonium, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium and by lightning.

questions.q: The carrying capacity of an environment is best defined as the:
options: Rate at which a population grows exponentially
Maximum population size that the environment can sustainably support
Minimum population needed to avoid extinction
Total number of trophic levels present
questions.explain: Carrying capacity (K) is the maximum population size that the available resources of an environment can support over time.

questions.q: A secondary consumer that feeds on a primary consumer occupies which trophic level, and which instrument best measures dissolved oxygen in its aquatic habitat?
options: Third trophic level; a dissolved oxygen meter
questions.explain: A secondary consumer is at the third trophic level, and dissolved oxygen in water is measured directly with a dissolved oxygen probe or meter.

questions.q: The competitive exclusion principle states that:
options: Two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely in the same habitat
Predators and prey cannot share a habitat
questions.explain: The competitive exclusion principle holds that two species with identical resource requirements cannot coexist stably; one outcompetes the other.

questions.q: The main reason food chains rarely exceed four or five trophic levels is that:
options: Decomposers consume all the energy first
So much energy is lost at each transfer that little remains to support higher levels
Sunlight cannot reach higher trophic levels
questions.explain: Because roughly 90% of energy is lost at each transfer, insufficient energy remains to sustain many trophic levels.

questions.q: In the nitrogen cycle, the process of nitrification involves:
options: Conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonium
Conversion of nitrate into nitrogen gas
Conversion of ammonium into nitrite and then nitrate by bacteria
Uptake of nitrate by plant roots
questions.explain: Nitrification is the oxidation of ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate by nitrifying bacteria such as Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter.

questions.q: K-strategist species are generally characterised by:
options: Few offspring, large body size, long lifespan and significant parental investment
Being the first colonisers of bare rock
Producing very large numbers of offspring with no parental care
questions.explain: K-strategists invest heavily in few offspring, are larger and longer-lived, and maintain populations near carrying capacity in stable habitats.

questions.q: The ecological niche of a species is best described as:
options: The total number of individuals in its population
The climax community it belongs to
The full role and position of a species, including its interactions and use of resources
Only the physical location where it lives
questions.explain: A niche encompasses an organism's role, resource use and interactions, not merely its habitat or physical address.

questions.q: An S-shaped (sigmoidal) population growth curve differs from a J-shaped curve because the S-curve:
options: Levels off as the population approaches carrying capacity
Always ends in a population crash
questions.explain: An S-curve shows growth slowing and stabilising near carrying capacity as limiting factors increase, unlike unchecked J-curve exponential growth.

questions.q: In a classic predator-prey relationship, a rise in the prey population is usually followed by:
options: A subsequent rise in the predator population
An immediate extinction of the predator
A permanent fall in prey numbers
questions.explain: More prey provides more food, so the predator population rises after a time lag, which then drives prey numbers back down, producing cyclic oscillations.

questions.q: As succession proceeds from pioneer to climax community, biodiversity and biomass generally:
questions.explain: Succession typically increases species diversity, biomass and complexity as soil develops and habitats become more stable.

questions.q: A J-shaped population growth curve is typically followed by:
options: A rapid population crash when resources are exhausted
No further change in population size
A stable plateau at carrying capacity
questions.explain: J-curve exponential growth often overshoots carrying capacity and is followed by a sharp crash as resources become limiting.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis fixes atmospheric CO2 into organic compounds, removing carbon from the atmosphere into living biomass.

questions.q: In a food chain, a herbivore that eats producers occupies which trophic level?
questions.explain: A primary consumer (herbivore) occupies the second trophic level, feeding directly on first-level producers.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of energy is typically transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain?
questions.explain: On average only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level, the rest being lost mainly through respiration, heat and egestion.

questions.q: Organisms that occupy the first trophic level of a food chain are the:
questions.explain: Producers (autotrophs) form the first trophic level, fixing energy through photosynthesis to support all higher levels.

questions.q: A pyramid of energy is always upright (broad base, narrow top) because:
options: Biomass increases with each trophic level
Energy is lost at each trophic transfer, so less is available higher up
There are always more individuals at lower levels
Producers are always physically larger than consumers
questions.explain: Energy decreases at every transfer, so a pyramid of energy is invariably upright, unlike pyramids of numbers or biomass which can be inverted.

questions.q: Gross primary productivity (GPP) refers to the:
options: Energy lost as heat from consumers
Total rate of energy fixed by producers in photosynthesis
Energy remaining in producers after respiration
questions.explain: GPP is the total rate at which producers convert light energy into chemical energy before any is lost to respiration.

questions.q: The final, relatively stable community reached at the end of a successional sequence is called the:
questions.explain: The climax community is the stable, self-sustaining end-point of succession, in equilibrium with prevailing environmental conditions.

questions.q: Which of the following is an abiotic factor in an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Soil pH is a non-living chemical factor, making it abiotic, whereas predation, competition and disease are biotic interactions.

questions.q: The first species to colonise bare rock in primary succession, such as lichens, are known as:
questions.explain: Pioneer species like lichens and mosses are the first colonisers, tolerating harsh conditions and beginning soil formation.

questions.q: Net primary productivity (NPP) is correctly calculated as:
questions.explain: NPP equals GPP minus the energy lost through plant respiration, representing the energy available to consumers as new biomass.

questions.q: Primary succession differs from secondary succession because primary succession:
options: Begins on previously colonised soil after a disturbance
Begins on newly exposed bare substrate with no pre-existing soil
Always reaches a climax community faster
Cannot result in a climax community
questions.explain: Primary succession starts on lifeless substrate such as bare rock or lava lacking soil, whereas secondary succession begins where soil already exists.

questions.q: A relationship in which both interacting species benefit, such as between bees and flowering plants, is called:
questions.explain: Mutualism is an interaction in which both species gain benefit, as when bees obtain nectar while pollinating plants.

questions.q: Which of the following is a density-dependent limiting factor on a population?
options: Competition for food as population density rises
questions.explain: Density-dependent factors such as competition, predation and disease intensify as population density increases, while climatic events are density-independent.

questions.q: A pyramid of numbers can appear inverted when:
options: Energy increases up the food chain
Many small producers support a few large consumers
One large producer such as a tree supports many smaller consumers
Decomposers are excluded from the count
questions.explain: A single large producer (e.g. an oak tree) can support many primary consumers (e.g. insects), giving a narrow base and inverted pyramid of numbers.
